Proposition B.14.

(Originally Proposition 2.5) LMowstL_{\text{{Mowst}}} upper-bounds LMowst⋆L_{\text{{Mowst}}}^{\star}.

Proof.

We compare Equation 1 and 3. Note that the loss LL is a convex function. In addition, C⁡(𝒑v)∈[0,1]C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\in[0,1]. Thus, C⁡(𝒑v)⋅𝒑v+(1−C⁡(𝒑v))⋅𝒑v′C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\cdot\bm{p}_{v}+\left(1-C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\right)\cdot\bm{p}_{v}^{\prime} is a convex combination of 𝒑v\bm{p}_{v} and 𝒑v′\bm{p}_{v}^{\prime} in LL’s domain.

Thus, by Definition B.1,

C⁡(𝒑v)⋅L⁡(𝒑v)+(1−C⁡(𝒑v))⋅L⁡(𝒑v′)≥L⁡(C⁡(𝒑v)⋅𝒑v+(1−C⁡(𝒑v))⋅𝒑v′)\displaystyle C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\cdot L\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)+\left(1-C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\right)\cdot L\left(\bm{p}_{v}^{\prime}\right)\geq L\left(C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\cdot\bm{p}_{v}+\left(1-C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\right)\cdot\bm{p}_{v}^{\prime}\right) (31)

B.2 Proofs related to expressive power

B.3 Proof of Proposition 2.6

Proposition B.15.

(Originally Proposition 2.6) Mowst and Mowst⋆\star are at least as expressive as the MLP or GNN expert alone.

Proof.

We complete the proof by showing a particular confidence function C=G∘DC=G\circ D and expert configuration, that reduce Mowst to an expert alone.

Define 𝒒v=C⁡(𝒑v)⋅𝒑v+(1−C⁡(𝒑v))⋅𝒑v′\bm{q}_{v}=C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\cdot\bm{p}_{v}+\left(1-C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\right)\cdot\bm{p}_{v}^{\prime}.

Further, define the following GG:

G⁡(x)={0,when ​x≤01,when ​x>0\displaystyle G(x)=\begin{cases}0,\qquad&\text{when }x\leq 0\\ 1,&\text{when }x>0\end{cases} (32)
Mowst⋆\star ⇒\Rightarrow MLP expert.

Let the GNN expert in our Mowst system always generate random prediction of 𝒑v′=1n​𝟏\bm{p}_{v}^{\prime}=\frac{1}{n}\bm{1}, regardless of vv. If the MLP expert does not generate a purely random guess (i.e., 𝒑v≠1n​𝟏\bm{p}_{v}\neq\frac{1}{n}\bm{1}), then D⁡(𝒑v)>0D\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)>0 according to Definition 2.1. So C⁡(𝒑v)=G⁡(D⁡(𝒑v))=1C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)=G\left(D\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\right)=1, and thus 𝒒v=𝒑v\bm{q}_{v}=\bm{p}_{v}. In the extreme case, where 𝒑v=1n​𝟏\bm{p}_{v}=\frac{1}{n}\bm{1}, we have 𝒒v=𝒑v′\bm{q}_{v}=\bm{p}_{v}^{\prime}. Yet, note that we configure our GNN expert to always output 1n​𝟏\frac{1}{n}\bm{1}. So we still have 𝒒v=𝒑v=1n​𝟏\bm{q}_{v}=\bm{p}_{v}=\frac{1}{n}\bm{1}. This shows that Mowst⋆\star can always produce identical output as an MLP alone.

Mowst⋆\star ⇒\Rightarrow GNN expert.

We configure the MLP expert such that it always generates a trivial prediction of 𝒑v=1n​𝟏\bm{p}_{v}=\frac{1}{n}\bm{1}. Then D⁡(𝒑v)=0D\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)=0 for all vv, and C⁡(𝒑v)=G⁡(D⁡(𝒑v))=0C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)=G\left(D\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\right)=0 for all vv according to Equation 32. So 𝒒v=𝒑v′\bm{q}_{v}=\bm{p}_{v}^{\prime}, and Mowst⋆\star always produces identical output as a GNN alone.

Cases for Mowst.

Similar reasoning can be applied to the Mowst design, where we can use the GG function defined in Equation 32 to let the Mowst system always predict according to the MLP expert alone, or the GNN expert alone (see Algorithm 1 for the inference operation).

B.3.1 Proof of Theorem 2.7

Theorem B.16.

(Originally Theorem 2.7) Mowst-GCN and Mowst⋆\star-GCN are more expressive than the GCN expert alone.

Proof.

By Proposition 2.6, we know that Mowst-GCN and Mowst⋆\star-GCN are at least as expressive as a GCN alone. To show that Mowst-GCN and Mowst⋆\star-GCN are more expressive than GCN, we only need to construct an example graph where 1. Mowst-GCNand Mowst⋆\star-GCN can differentiate all nodes that a GCN can differentiate, and 2. Mowst-GCNand Mowst⋆\star-GCN can differentiate some nodes that any GCN cannot differentiate.

Suppose the GCN has KK layers. We construct a graph 𝒢⁡(𝒱,ℰ,𝑿)\mathcal{G}\left(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\bm{X}\right) as follows. Consider two sets of nodes 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} and 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2}, where v∈𝒮1v\in\mathcal{S}_{1} has label yy and v∈𝒮2v\in\mathcal{S}_{2} has label y′y^{\prime} (y≠y′y\neq y^{\prime}). Denote 𝒩vk\mathcal{N}_{v}^{k} as the set of neighbor nodes that are kk hops away from vv (let 𝒩v0={v}\mathcal{N}_{v}^{0}=\{v\}). We further enforce the following two constraints:

  1. (1).

    For any u∈𝒮1u\in\mathcal{S}_{1} and v∈𝒮2v\in\mathcal{S}_{2}, their KK-hop neighborhood do not overlap. i.e., (⋃0≤k≤K𝒩uk)∩(⋃0≤k≤K𝒩vk)=∅\left(\bigcup_{0\leq k\leq K}\mathcal{N}_{u}^{k}\right)\cap\left(\bigcup_{0\leq k\leq K}\mathcal{N}_{v}^{k}\right)=\emptyset

  2. (2).

    For any v∈𝒮1∪𝒮2v\in\mathcal{S}_{1}\cup\mathcal{S}_{2} and for any u∈𝒩vku\in\mathcal{N}_{v}^{k} (where 1≤k≤K−11\leq k\leq K-1), there exist some edge (u,w)∈ℰ\left(u,w\right)\in\mathcal{E} where w∈𝒩vk+1w\in\mathcal{N}_{v}^{k+1}.

Next, we discuss how to set the node features. We first review the operation of a GCN layer. For a node vv in layer kk, the GCN performs weighted sum of the embedding vectors of vv’s direct neighbors in layer (k−1)\left(k-1\right). Denote 𝒉v(k)\bm{h}_{v}^{\left(k\right)} as the output embedding vector of vv in layer kk. Then

𝒉v(k)=σ⁡((𝑾(k))𝖳⋅∑u∈𝒩v1∪{v}1(deg​(u)+1)⋅(deg​(v)+1)​𝒉u(k−1))\displaystyle\bm{h}_{v}^{\left(k\right)}=\sigma\left(\left(\bm{W}^{\left(k\right)}\right)^{\mathsf{T}}\cdot\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}_{v}^{1}\cup\{v\}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\left({\text{deg}\left(u\right)}+1\right)\cdot\left({\text{deg}\left(v\right)}+1\right)}}\bm{h}_{u}^{\left(k-1\right)}\right) (33)

where σ\sigma is the activation function, 𝑾(k)\bm{W}^{\left(k\right)} is the learnable weight matrix of layer kk, and deg​(⋅){\text{deg}\left(\cdot\right)} gives the degree of the node.

Denote 𝒙v=𝒉v(0)\bm{x}_{v}=\bm{h}_{v}^{\left(0\right)} as the raw node feature. We can construct the graph features such that ∑u∈𝒩v1∪{v}1(deg​(u)+1)⋅(deg​(v)+1)​𝒉u(0)=𝟎\sum_{u\in\mathcal{N}_{v}^{1}\cup\{v\}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\left({\text{deg}\left(u\right)}+1\right)\cdot\left({\text{deg}\left(v\right)}+1\right)}}\bm{h}_{u}^{\left(0\right)}=\bm{0} for all v∈⋃0≤k≤K−1𝒩vkv\in\bigcup_{0\leq k\leq K-1}\mathcal{N}_{v}^{k}. This can be achieved due to the constraint (2) above: for each u∈𝒩vku\in\mathcal{N}_{v}^{k}, we can set the feature of uu’s neighbor(s) in 𝒩vk+1\mathcal{N}_{v}^{k+1} so that it “counter-acts” the features for uu’s neighbor(s) in 𝒩vk∪𝒩vk−1\mathcal{N}_{v}^{k}\cup\mathcal{N}_{v}^{k-1}. i.e., ∑w∈𝒩u1∩𝒩vk+11(deg​(w)+1)⋅(deg​(u)+1)⋅𝒉w(0)=∑w′∈𝒩u1∩(𝒩vk∪𝒩vk−1)1(deg​(w′)+1)⋅(deg​(u)+1)⋅𝒉w′(0)\sum_{w\in\mathcal{N}_{u}^{1}\cap\mathcal{N}_{v}^{k+1}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\left({\text{deg}\left(w\right)}+1\right)\cdot\left({\text{deg}\left(u\right)}+1\right)}}\cdot\bm{h}_{w}^{\left(0\right)}=\sum_{w^{\prime}\in\mathcal{N}_{u}^{1}\cap\left(\mathcal{N}_{v}^{k}\cup\mathcal{N}_{v}^{k-1}\right)}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\left({\text{deg}\left(w^{\prime}\right)}+1\right)\cdot\left({\text{deg}\left(u\right)}+1\right)}}\cdot\bm{h}_{w^{\prime}}^{\left(0\right)}.

When we configure the KK-hop neighbors in this way, it is easy to see that for any two nodes v,u∈𝒮1∪𝒮2v,u\in\mathcal{S}_{1}\cup\mathcal{S}_{2}, all possible KK-layer GCN will always output the same prediction. This can be seen by an induction process. In layer 1, the model aggregates 𝒉w(0)\bm{h}_{w}^{\left(0\right)} from all w∈(⋃0≤k≤K𝒩uk)∪(⋃0≤k≤K𝒩vk)w\in\left(\bigcup_{0\leq k\leq{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}K}}\mathcal{N}_{u}^{k}\right)\cup\left(\bigcup_{0\leq k\leq{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}K}}\mathcal{N}_{v}^{k}\right). Nodes w∈(⋃0≤k≤K−1𝒩uk)∪(⋃0≤k≤K−1𝒩vk)w\in\left(\bigcup_{0\leq k\leq{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}K-1}}\mathcal{N}_{u}^{k}\right)\cup\left(\bigcup_{0\leq k\leq{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}K-1}}\mathcal{N}_{v}^{k}\right) gets 𝟎\bm{0} from the neighbor aggregation, and thus all such ww have identical layer-1 output embeddings. In layer 2, the model aggregates 𝒉w(1)\bm{h}_{w}^{\left(1\right)} from w∈(⋃0≤k≤K−1𝒩uk)∪(⋃0≤k≤K−1𝒩vk)w\in\left(\bigcup_{0\leq k\leq{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}K-1}}\mathcal{N}_{u}^{k}\right)\cup\left(\bigcup_{0\leq k\leq{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}K-1}}\mathcal{N}_{v}^{k}\right) and gets 𝟎\bm{0}, so all w∈(⋃0≤k≤K−2𝒩uk)∪(⋃0≤k≤K−2𝒩vk)w\in\left(\bigcup_{0\leq k\leq{\color[rgb]{0,1,0}K-2}}\mathcal{N}_{u}^{k}\right)\cup\left(\bigcup_{0\leq k\leq{\color[rgb]{0,1,0}K-2}}\mathcal{N}_{v}^{k}\right) have identical 𝒉w(2)\bm{h}_{w}^{\left(2\right)}. Following this reasoning, 𝒉v(K)\bm{h}_{v}^{\left(K\right)} and 𝒉u(K)\bm{h}_{u}^{\left(K\right)} output from the last GCN layer must be the same. So it is impossible for any KK-layer GCN to differentiate nodes in 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} from those in 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2}.

Now consider Mowst-GCN and Mowst⋆\star-GCN. For simplicity, consider that for all u∈𝒮1u\in\mathcal{S}_{1}, they have identical self-feature 𝒙w=𝒙1\bm{x}_{w}=\bm{x}_{1}. For all w∈𝒮2w\in\mathcal{S}_{2}, they also have identical self-feature 𝒙w=𝒙2\bm{x}_{w}=\bm{x}_{2}. And 𝒙1≠𝒙2\bm{x}_{1}\neq\bm{x}_{2}. In addition, for all other nodes w∈𝒱−𝒮1−𝒮2w\in\mathcal{V}-\mathcal{S}_{1}-\mathcal{S}_{2} that we want to predict, they have self-features not equal to 𝒙1\bm{x}_{1} or 𝒙2\bm{x}_{2}. Consider the following confidence function defined by

G⁡(x)={0,when ​x≤01,when ​x>0\displaystyle G(x)=\begin{cases}0,\qquad&\text{when }x\leq 0\\ 1,&\text{when }x>0\end{cases} (34)

We can have an MLP expert which only differentiates nodes in 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} and 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2} based on the input feature 𝒙1\bm{x}_{1} and 𝒙2\bm{x}_{2}, and always produces a 1n​𝟏\frac{1}{n}\bm{1} prediction for all other target nodes. This is doable because target nodes not in 𝒮1∪𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{1}\cup\mathcal{S}_{2} have different self-features. In this case, for nodes in 𝒮1∪𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{1}\cup\mathcal{S}_{2}, the MLP’s prediction has positive dispersion and so G=1G=1. This means that the confidence function acts like a binary gate to completely disable the GCN expert. Otherwise, the MLP’s prediction has zero dispersion and so G=0G=0. The confidence function completely disable the MLP expert and rely on the GCN expert. Under the above configuration, Mowst-GCN and Mowst⋆\star-GCN can differentiate all nodes that a GCN model can differentiate, and they can also differentiate nodes that any GCN model cannot differentiate (𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} vs. 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2}). This proves that Mowst-GCN and Mowst⋆\star-GCN are strictly more expressive than a GCN alone. ∎

B.3.2 Proof of Proposition 2.8

Proposition B.17.

(Originally Proposition 2.8) Mowst and Mowst⋆\star are at least as expressive as any expert alone.

Proof.

The proof follows the idea of proving Proposition 2.8.

The logic to prove the case of Mowst is identical to that of Mowst⋆\star, and thus we only discuss the Mowst case in detail. Consider a confidence function C=G∘DC=G\circ D defined by:

G⁡(x)={0,when ​x≤01,when ​x>0\displaystyle G(x)=\begin{cases}0,\qquad&\text{when }x\leq 0\\ 1,&\text{when }x>0\end{cases} (35)

Equation 40 defines the general form for Mowst consisting of MM experts. The coefficient in front of the LmvL_{m}^{v} loss, τmv≔(∏1≤i<m(1−Civ))⋅Cmv\tau_{m}^{v}\coloneqq\left(\prod\limits_{1\leq i<m}\left(1-C_{i}^{v}\right)\right)\cdot C_{m}^{v} , defines the probability of activating expert mm during inference (i.e., we can easily generalize Algorithm 1 based on Equation 40). If we want the whole Mowst system to produce identical results as the mm-th expert, we (roughly) need to show that τmv=1\tau_{m}^{v}=1 for all vv, and τm′v=0\tau_{m^{\prime}}^{v}=0 (except some corner case that we will separately discuss).

For m′≠mm^{\prime}\neq m, we always let the expert m′m^{\prime} to generate random guess of 1n​𝟏\frac{1}{n}\bm{1} for all vv. Note that a 1n​𝟏\frac{1}{n}\bm{1} prediction corresponds to a 0 dispersion, and thus the corresponding GG and CC are also 0. A prediction not equal to 1n​𝟏\frac{1}{n}\bm{1} leads to positive dispersion, and thus a confidence of 1. Since the confidence value in our setup is binary, then if we want τm′v=0\tau_{m^{\prime}}^{v}=0 for some 1≤m′≤M1\leq m^{\prime}\leq M, we either need its own Cm′v=0C_{m^{\prime}}^{v}=0, or at least one of its preceding experts to have Cm′′v=1C_{m^{\prime\prime}}^{v}=1 (for some m′′<m′m^{\prime\prime}<m^{\prime}). If we want τm′v=1\tau_{m^{\prime}}^{v}=1 for some 1≤m′≤M1\leq m^{\prime}\leq M, we need all its preceding experts to have Cm′′v=0C_{m^{\prime\prime}}^{v}=0 (for all m′′<m′m^{\prime\prime}<m^{\prime}) as well as Cm′v=1C_{m^{\prime}}^{v}=1.

According to the above categorization, for expert m′m^{\prime} where m′<mm^{\prime}<m, we always have their τm′v=0\tau_{m^{\prime}}^{v}=0 since Cm′v=0C_{m^{\prime}}^{v}=0. If expert mm generates a non-1n​𝟏\frac{1}{n}\bm{1} prediction, then τmv=1\tau_{m}^{v}=1 and thus the whole Mowst system degrades to a single expert mm. If expert mm predicts 1n​𝟏\frac{1}{n}\bm{1}, then τMv=1\tau_{M}^{v}=1 (since by definition, CMv=1C_{M}^{v}=1 for all vv). Since the expert MM also predicts 1n​𝟏\frac{1}{n}\bm{1}, the system’s output is also equivalent to expert mm’s output.

Thus, Mowst and Mowst⋆\star can produce identical results as any expert alone.

∎

Appendix C Additional Algorithmic Details

C.1 Derivation of the optimization problem 2

We re-write LMowstL_{\text{{Mowst}}} (Equation 1) as follows:

LMowst=\displaystyle L_{\text{{Mowst}}}= 1|𝒱|​∑v∈𝒱(C⁡(𝒑v)⋅L⁡(𝒑v,𝒚v)+(1−C⁡(𝒑v))⋅L⁡(𝒑v′,𝒚v))\displaystyle\frac{1}{\left\lvert\mathcal{V}\right\rvert}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\big(C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\cdot L\left(\bm{p}_{v},\bm{y}_{v}\right)+\left(1-C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\right)\cdot L\left(\bm{p}^{\prime}_{v},\bm{y}_{v}\right)\big)
=\displaystyle= 1|𝒱|​∑v∈𝒱(C⁡(𝒑v)⋅(L⁡(𝒑v,𝒚v)−L⁡(𝒑v′,𝒚v))+L⁡(𝒑v′,𝒚v))\displaystyle\frac{1}{\left\lvert\mathcal{V}\right\rvert}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\big(C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\cdot\left(L\left(\bm{p}_{v},\bm{y}_{v}\right)-L\left(\bm{p}_{v}^{\prime},\bm{y}_{v}\right)\right)+L\left(\bm{p}_{v}^{\prime},\bm{y}_{v}\right)\big)
=\displaystyle= 1|𝒱|​∑v∈𝒱C⁡(𝒑v)⋅(L⁡(𝒑v,𝒚v)−L⁡(𝒑v′,𝒚v))+1|𝒱|​∑v∈𝒱L⁡(𝒑v′,𝒚v)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\left\lvert\mathcal{V}\right\rvert}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\cdot\left(L\left(\bm{p}_{v},\bm{y}_{v}\right)-L\left(\bm{p}_{v}^{\prime},\bm{y}_{v}\right)\right)+\frac{1}{\left\lvert\mathcal{V}\right\rvert}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}L\left(\bm{p}_{v}^{\prime},\bm{y}_{v}\right) (36)

Since we optimize the MLP parameters by fixing the GNN, L⁡(𝒑v′,𝒚v)L\left(\bm{p}_{v}^{\prime},\bm{y}_{v}\right) remains constant throughout the process. So:

arg⁡min{𝒑v}⁡LMowst=arg⁡min{𝒑v}​∑v∈𝒱C⁡(𝒑v)⋅(L⁡(𝒑v,𝒚v)−L⁡(𝒑v′,𝒚v))\displaystyle\arg\min_{\{\bm{p}_{v}\}}L_{\text{{Mowst}}}=\arg\min_{\{\bm{p}_{v}\}}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\cdot\left(L\left(\bm{p}_{v},\bm{y}_{v}\right)-L\left(\bm{p}_{v}^{\prime},\bm{y}_{v}\right)\right) (37)

Now we simplify as follows:

∑v∈𝒱C⁡(𝒑v)⋅(L⁡(𝒑v,𝒚v)−L⁡(𝒑v′,𝒚v))\displaystyle\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\cdot\left(L\left(\bm{p}_{v},\bm{y}_{v}\right)-L\left(\bm{p}_{v}^{\prime},\bm{y}_{v}\right)\right)
=\displaystyle= ∑1≤i≤m∑v∈ℳiC⁡(𝒑v)⋅(L⁡(𝒑v,𝒚v)−L⁡(𝒑v′,𝒚v))\displaystyle\sum_{1\leq i\leq m}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{M}_{i}}C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\cdot\left(L\left(\bm{p}_{v},\bm{y}_{v}\right)-L\left(\bm{p}_{v}^{\prime},\bm{y}_{v}\right)\right)
=\displaystyle= ∑1≤i≤m∑v∈ℳiC⁡(𝒑v)⋅L⁡(𝒑v,𝒚v)−∑1≤i≤m∑v∈ℳiC⁡(𝒑v)⋅L⁡(𝒑v′,𝒚v)\displaystyle\sum_{1\leq i\leq m}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{M}_{i}}C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\cdot L\left(\bm{p}_{v},\bm{y}_{v}\right)-\sum_{1\leq i\leq m}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{M}_{i}}C\left(\bm{p}_{v}\right)\cdot L\left(\bm{p}_{v}^{\prime},\bm{y}_{v}\right)
=\displaystyle= ∑1≤i≤mC⁡(𝒑^i)⋅(∑v∈ℳiL⁡(𝒑^i,𝒚v))−∑1≤i≤mC⁡(𝒑^i)⋅(∑v∈ℳiL⁡(𝒑v′,𝒚v))\displaystyle\sum_{1\leq i\leq m}C\left(\hat{\bm{p}}_{i}\right)\cdot\left(\sum_{v\in\mathcal{M}_{i}}L\left(\hat{\bm{p}}_{i},\bm{y}_{v}\right)\right)-\sum_{1\leq i\leq m}C\left(\hat{\bm{p}}_{i}\right)\cdot\left(\sum_{v\in\mathcal{M}_{i}}L\left(\bm{p}_{v}^{\prime},\bm{y}_{v}\right)\right)
=\displaystyle= ∑1≤i≤mC⁡(𝒑^i)⋅(∑v∈ℳiL⁡(𝒑^i,𝒚v)−∑v∈ℳiL⁡(𝒑v′,𝒚v))\displaystyle\sum_{1\leq i\leq m}C\left(\hat{\bm{p}}_{i}\right)\cdot\left(\sum_{v\in\mathcal{M}_{i}}L\left(\hat{\bm{p}}_{i},\bm{y}_{v}\right)-\sum_{v\in\mathcal{M}_{i}}L\left(\bm{p}_{v}^{\prime},\bm{y}_{v}\right)\right)
=\displaystyle= ∑1≤i≤mC⁡(𝒑^i)⋅(|ℳi|⋅L^𝜶i​(𝒑^i)−|ℳi|⋅μi)\displaystyle\sum_{1\leq i\leq m}C\left(\hat{\bm{p}}_{i}\right)\cdot\left(\left\lvert\mathcal{M}_{i}\right\rvert\cdot\hat{L}_{\bm{\alpha}_{i}}\left(\hat{\bm{p}}_{i}\right)-\left\lvert\mathcal{M}_{i}\right\rvert\cdot\mu_{i}\right)
=\displaystyle= |ℳi|​∑1≤i≤mC⁡(𝒑^i)⋅(L^𝜶i​(𝒑^i)−μi)\displaystyle\left\lvert\mathcal{M}_{i}\right\rvert\sum_{1\leq i\leq m}C\left(\hat{\bm{p}}_{i}\right)\cdot\left(\hat{L}_{\bm{\alpha}_{i}}\left(\hat{\bm{p}}_{i}\right)-\mu_{i}\right) (38)

where Equation 38 is (almost) exactly our objective in optimization problem 2, with the only difference being the scaling factor |ℳi|\left\lvert\mathcal{M}_{i}\right\rvert. We can use the “decomposible” argument in Appendix B.1.3 to easily derive that this scaling factor does not affect the optimizer 𝒑^i∗\hat{\bm{p}}_{i}^{*}.

C.2 Extending to more than two experts

Following the notations in §2.7, we first have the case of 3 agents:

LMowst=\displaystyle L_{\text{{Mowst}}}= 1|𝒱|​∑v∈𝒱(C1v⋅L1v+(1−C1v)⋅(C2v⋅L2v+(1−C2v)⋅L3v))\displaystyle\frac{1}{\left\lvert\mathcal{V}\right\rvert}\sum\limits_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\left(C_{1}^{v}\cdot L_{1}^{v}+\left(1-C_{1}^{v}\right)\cdot\left(C_{2}^{v}\cdot L_{2}^{v}+\left(1-C_{2}^{v}\right)\cdot L_{3}^{v}\right)\right)
=\displaystyle= 1|𝒱|​∑v∈𝒱(C1v⋅L1v+(1−C1v)⋅C2v⋅L2v+(1−C1v)​(1−C2v)⋅L3v)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\left\lvert\mathcal{V}\right\rvert}\sum\limits_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\left(C_{1}^{v}\cdot L_{1}^{v}+\left(1-C_{1}^{v}\right)\cdot C_{2}^{v}\cdot L_{2}^{v}+\left(1-C_{1}^{v}\right)\left(1-C_{2}^{v}\right)\cdot L_{3}^{v}\right) (39)

In general, for MM experts, we have the following loss:

LMowst=1|𝒱|​∑v∈𝒱∑1≤m≤M(∏1≤i<m(1−Civ))⋅Cmv⋅Lmv\displaystyle L_{\text{{Mowst}}}=\frac{1}{\left\lvert\mathcal{V}\right\rvert}\sum\limits_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\sum\limits_{1\leq m\leq M}\left(\prod\limits_{1\leq i<m}\left(1-C_{i}^{v}\right)\right)\cdot C_{m}^{v}\cdot L_{m}^{v} (40)

where we define ∏x≤i<x(1−Civ)=1\prod_{x\leq i<x}\left(1-C_{i}^{v}\right)=1 for any integer xx.

We further define the following term:

L≥qv=∑q≤m≤M(∏q≤i<m(1−Civ))⋅Cmv⋅Lmv\displaystyle L_{\geq q}^{v}=\sum\limits_{q\leq m\leq M}\left(\prod\limits_{q\leq i<m}\left(1-C_{i}^{v}\right)\right)\cdot C_{m}^{v}\cdot L_{m}^{v} (41)

So LMowst=1|𝒱|​∑v∈𝒱L≥1vL_{\text{{Mowst}}}=\frac{1}{\left\lvert\mathcal{V}\right\rvert}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}L_{\geq 1}^{v} and L≥qv=Cqv⋅Lqv+(1−Cqv)⋅L≥q+1vL_{\geq q}^{v}=C_{q}^{v}\cdot L_{q}^{v}+\left(1-C_{q}^{v}\right)\cdot L_{\geq q+1}^{v} defines the basic recursive formulation.
